questions.question: In an elementary reaction step proceeding with 100% retention of stereochemistry, what is the spatial trajectory of the incoming group?

options.label: A
options.text: The stereocenter is destroyed permanently.

options.label: B
options.text: The incoming group attacks from the exact same face from which the leaving group departs, preserving spatial orientation.

options.label: C
options.text: The incoming group attacks 180° opposite the leaving group.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a free planar carbocation.

questions.correct_answer: The incoming group attacks from the exact same face from which the leaving group departs, preserving spatial orientation.
questions.explanation: Frontside attack or concerted migration with retention preserves the 3D configuration of the stereocenter.

questions.question: Why does nucleophilic capture of an unhindered secondary carbocation typically yield a racemic mixture?

options.label: A
options.text: The product undergoes spontaneous optical rotation.

options.label: B
options.text: The carbocation rapidly inverts like an umbrella.

options.label: C
options.text: The leaving group forces attack from one face only.

options.label: D
options.text: The carbocation carbon is sp² hybridized with a planar trigonal geometry and an unhybridized 2p orbital, allowing nucleophilic attack with equal probability from top and bottom faces.

questions.correct_answer: The carbocation carbon is sp² hybridized with a planar trigonal geometry and an unhybridized 2p orbital, allowing nucleophilic attack with equal probability from top and bottom faces.
questions.explanation: Planar sp² carbocations are achiral; attack from either enantiotopic face occurs with equal probability, yielding a 50:50 racemic mixture.

questions.question: What does the term 'stereoelectronic control' mean in organic reaction mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.text: The rule that all stereocenters must be (R) configured.

options.label: B
options.text: The concept that only nonpolar molecules can react.

options.label: C
options.text: The requirement that participating orbitals must achieve a specific geometric alignment (e.g., anti-periplanar or collinear) in the transition state to minimize activation energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The requirement that all reactions must be carried out at 0°C.

questions.correct_answer: The requirement that participating orbitals must achieve a specific geometric alignment (e.g., anti-periplanar or collinear) in the transition state to minimize activation energy.
questions.explanation: Stereoelectronic factors dictate that optimal orbital overlap in the transition state governs the stereochemical pathway of the reaction.

questions.question: How does the Hammond Postulate relate transition state geometry to intermediate structure in an endergonic step?

options.label: A
options.text: The transition state occurs late and geometrically resembles the higher-energy intermediate or product more closely than the starting material.

options.label: B
options.text: The transition state resembles the starting materials.

options.label: C
options.text: The transition state resembles the solvent.

options.label: D
options.text: The transition state is completely flat.

questions.correct_answer: The transition state occurs late and geometrically resembles the higher-energy intermediate or product more closely than the starting material.
questions.explanation: Endergonic steps have late transition states that structurally and energetically resemble the adjacent high-energy intermediate.

questions.topic: Energy Profiles of Diastereomeric Transition States
questions.question: Why do two enantiomers react at different rates with a chiral reagent or enzyme?

options.label: A
options.text: The two transition states are diastereomeric, having different free energies of activation (ΔG₁‡ ≠ ΔG₂‡) and leading to kinetic resolution.

options.label: B
options.text: Enantiomers have different boiling points.

options.label: C
options.text: Chiral reagents destroy one enantiomer by heat.

options.label: D
options.text: Enantiomers have different molecular formulas.

questions.correct_answer: The two transition states are diastereomeric, having different free energies of activation (ΔG₁‡ ≠ ΔG₂‡) and leading to kinetic resolution.
questions.explanation: Interaction of chiral substrates with chiral reagents creates diastereomeric transition states with different activation barriers.

questions.question: Why does an optically active ketone with a chiral α-carbon [(R)-3-phenyl-2-butanone] lose its optical activity in acid or base?

options.label: A
options.text: The phenyl group falls off as a radical.

options.label: B
options.text: The ketone decomposes into benzene and acetone.

options.label: C
options.text: The carbonyl group is oxidized to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: D
options.text: Tautomerization forms an achiral, planar enol/enolate intermediate (sp² at α-carbon); reprotonation from top or bottom faces occurs with equal probability, causing racemization.

questions.correct_answer: Tautomerization forms an achiral, planar enol/enolate intermediate (sp² at α-carbon); reprotonation from top or bottom faces occurs with equal probability, causing racemization.
questions.explanation: Enolization flattens the chiral α-carbon into an achiral sp² plane; reprotonation yields an equimolar racemic mixture.

questions.question: What does microscopic reversibility imply about the stereochemical pathway of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction?

options.label: A
options.text: The enzyme is destroyed after one turnover.

options.label: B
options.text: The reverse reaction must proceed with inversion if the forward reaction had retention.

options.label: C
options.text: The reverse reaction cannot occur in the same cell.

options.label: D
options.text: The enzyme must catalyze the reverse reaction through the exact same stereochemical trajectory and transition states in reverse order.

questions.correct_answer: The enzyme must catalyze the reverse reaction through the exact same stereochemical trajectory and transition states in reverse order.
questions.explanation: The forward and reverse reaction paths share the exact same potential energy surface and stereochemical geometry.

questions.question: What is the maximum theoretical yield of a single pure enantiomer obtained from a classical kinetic resolution of a racemate?

options.label: A
options.text: 100% yield.

options.label: B
options.text: 75% yield.

options.label: C
options.text: 25% yield.

options.label: D
options.text: 50% maximum theoretical yield, because the chiral catalyst selectively converts only one of the two enantiomers in the 50:50 mixture.

questions.correct_answer: 50% maximum theoretical yield, because the chiral catalyst selectively converts only one of the two enantiomers in the 50:50 mixture.
questions.explanation: Kinetic resolution differentiates between two enantiomers, reacting with one fast while leaving the other (50% max recovery).

questions.question: In cyclohexyl systems, why does the Curtin-Hammett principle state that product distribution is NOT determined by ground-state conformer populations?

options.label: A
options.text: Chair flips cannot occur during chemical reactions.

options.label: B
options.text: Ground-state populations always dictate 100% of product ratio.

options.label: C
options.text: All conformers have identical transition state energies.

options.label: D
options.text: When conformational interconversion is much faster than the reaction, product ratio depends solely on the relative energies of the transition states (ΔΔG‡), not ground-state ratios.

questions.correct_answer: When conformational interconversion is much faster than the reaction, product ratio depends solely on the relative energies of the transition states (ΔΔG‡), not ground-state ratios.
questions.explanation: The Curtin-Hammett principle demonstrates that product ratios depend on transition state free energies when conformers equilibrate rapidly.

options.text: The Felkin-Anh model, which places the largest α-substituent perpendicular to the carbonyl and directs nucleophilic attack at the Bürgi-Dunitz angle from the least hindered trajectory.

options.label: B
options.text: The Markovnikov rule.

options.label: C
options.text: The Zaitsev rule.

options.label: D
options.text: The Hofmann elimination rule.

questions.question: Why does an optically active ketone with a chiral α-carbon [(R)-3-phenyl-2-butanone] lose its optical activity in acid or base?

options.text: The phenyl group falls off as a radical.

options.text: The ketone decomposes into benzene and acetone.

options.label: D
options.text: Tautomerization forms an achiral, planar enol/enolate intermediate (sp² at α-carbon); reprotonation from top or bottom faces occurs with equal probability, causing racemization.

questions.correct_answer: Tautomerization forms an achiral, planar enol/enolate intermediate (sp² at α-carbon); reprotonation from top or bottom faces occurs with equal probability, causing racemization.
questions.explanation: Enolization flattens the chiral α-carbon into an achiral sp² plane; reprotonation yields an equimolar racemic mixture.

questions.question: In cyclohexyl systems, why does the Curtin-Hammett principle state that product distribution is NOT determined by ground-state conformer populations?

options.label: A
options.text: Ground-state populations always dictate 100% of product ratio.

options.label: B
options.text: Chair flips cannot occur during chemical reactions.

options.label: C
options.text: When conformational interconversion is much faster than the reaction, product ratio depends solely on the relative energies of the transition states (ΔΔG‡), not ground-state ratios.

options.label: D
options.text: All conformers have identical transition state energies.

questions.correct_answer: When conformational interconversion is much faster than the reaction, product ratio depends solely on the relative energies of the transition states (ΔΔG‡), not ground-state ratios.
questions.explanation: The Curtin-Hammett principle demonstrates that product ratios depend on transition state free energies when conformers equilibrate rapidly.

questions.question: What model predicts the diastereoselective nucleophilic addition to a chiral aldehyde carbonyl?

options.label: A
options.text: The Markovnikov rule.

options.label: B
options.text: The Felkin-Anh model, which places the largest α-substituent perpendicular to the carbonyl and directs nucleophilic attack at the Bürgi-Dunitz angle from the least hindered trajectory.

options.label: C
options.text: The Zaitsev rule.

options.label: D
options.text: The Hofmann elimination rule.

questions.correct_answer: The Felkin-Anh model, which places the largest α-substituent perpendicular to the carbonyl and directs nucleophilic attack at the Bürgi-Dunitz angle from the least hindered trajectory.
questions.explanation: The Felkin-Anh transition state model accounts for steric and stereoelectronic factors governing diastereoselective carbonyl addition.

questions.question: In an elementary reaction step proceeding with 100% retention of stereochemistry, what is the spatial trajectory of the incoming group?

options.text: The incoming group attacks 180° opposite the leaving group.

options.label: C
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a free planar carbocation.

options.label: D
options.text: The incoming group attacks from the exact same face from which the leaving group departs, preserving spatial orientation.

questions.correct_answer: The incoming group attacks from the exact same face from which the leaving group departs, preserving spatial orientation.
questions.explanation: Frontside attack or concerted migration with retention preserves the 3D configuration of the stereocenter.

questions.question: Why does nucleophilic capture of an unhindered secondary carbocation typically yield a racemic mixture?

options.label: A
options.text: The leaving group forces attack from one face only.

options.label: B
options.text: The carbocation carbon is sp² hybridized with a planar trigonal geometry and an unhybridized 2p orbital, allowing nucleophilic attack with equal probability from top and bottom faces.

options.label: C
options.text: The product undergoes spontaneous optical rotation.

options.label: D
options.text: The carbocation rapidly inverts like an umbrella.

questions.correct_answer: The carbocation carbon is sp² hybridized with a planar trigonal geometry and an unhybridized 2p orbital, allowing nucleophilic attack with equal probability from top and bottom faces.
questions.explanation: Planar sp² carbocations are achiral; attack from either enantiotopic face occurs with equal probability, yielding a 50:50 racemic mixture.

questions.question: What does the term 'stereoelectronic control' mean in organic reaction mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.text: The concept that only nonpolar molecules can react.

options.label: B
options.text: The requirement that participating orbitals must achieve a specific geometric alignment (e.g., anti-periplanar or collinear) in the transition state to minimize activation energy.

options.label: C
options.text: The requirement that all reactions must be carried out at 0°C.

options.label: D
options.text: The rule that all stereocenters must be (R) configured.

questions.correct_answer: The requirement that participating orbitals must achieve a specific geometric alignment (e.g., anti-periplanar or collinear) in the transition state to minimize activation energy.
questions.explanation: Stereoelectronic factors dictate that optimal orbital overlap in the transition state governs the stereochemical pathway of the reaction.

questions.question: How does the Hammond Postulate relate transition state geometry to intermediate structure in an endergonic step?

options.text: The transition state occurs late and geometrically resembles the higher-energy intermediate or product more closely than the starting material.

options.label: B
options.text: The transition state resembles the solvent.

options.label: C
options.text: The transition state is completely flat.

options.label: D
options.text: The transition state resembles the starting materials.

questions.correct_answer: The transition state occurs late and geometrically resembles the higher-energy intermediate or product more closely than the starting material.
questions.explanation: Endergonic steps have late transition states that structurally and energetically resemble the adjacent high-energy intermediate.
